title: Biochemical Reasoning
source_note: Integrative case-based bank synthesizing standard clinical biochemistry, metabolic disease biochemistry, and experimental biochemistry principles (inborn errors of metabolism, acid-base physiology, enzymology, endocrine-metabolic regulation) as commonly taught in 400-level Biochemistry problem-solving/case-study courses; reference lab values are standard adult ranges, not LASU-specific.

questions.question: A 6-month-old infant presents with vomiting, lethargy, and a musty odor to the urine after starting solid foods containing wheat and dairy. Plasma amino acid analysis shows markedly elevated phenylalanine with low tyrosine. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
options: Phenylalanine hydroxylase
Tyrosine aminotransferase
Homogentisate oxidase
Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase
questions.correct_answer: Phenylalanine hydroxylase
questions.explanation: Deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase (or its cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin) blocks conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine, causing phenylalanine and its ketone by-products (which give the musty odor) to accumulate, the classic picture of phenylketonuria.

questions.question: A newborn becomes lethargic and tachypneic 48 hours after birth, with respiratory alkalosis, markedly elevated plasma ammonia, and low blood urea nitrogen, but normal anion gap and no ketosis. Plasma citrulline is very low and urine orotic acid is low. Which urea cycle enzyme defect best fits this picture?
options: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency
Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency
Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency
Arginase deficiency
questions.correct_answer: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency
questions.explanation: CPS I is the first, rate-limiting urea cycle enzyme; its deficiency causes hyperammonemia with low citrulline (since little carbamoyl phosphate is made) and low urine orotic acid, distinguishing it from OTC deficiency where excess carbamoyl phosphate is shunted into orotic acid overproduction.

questions.question: A urea cycle disorder patient shows hyperammonemia together with markedly elevated urine orotic acid. This combination localizes the defect to which enzyme, and why?
options: Ornithine transcarbamylase, because accumulated carbamoyl phosphate is diverted into the cytosolic pyrimidine synthesis pathway
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, because no carbamoyl phosphate is available for orotic acid synthesis
Arginase, because arginine accumulation directly stimulates orotic acid production
N-acetylglutamate synthase, because loss of CPS I activation prevents orotic acid clearance
questions.correct_answer: Ornithine transcarbamylase, because accumulated carbamoyl phosphate is diverted into the cytosolic pyrimidine synthesis pathway
questions.explanation: In OTC deficiency, mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate cannot be used to form citrulline and leaks into the cytosol, where it feeds the pyrimidine synthesis pathway, raising orotic acid, an X-linked finding used to distinguish OTC deficiency from CPS I deficiency.

questions.question: An infant's urine has a sweet, burnt-sugar odor, and feeding leads to poor feeding, lethargy, and hypoglycemia. Plasma shows elevated leucine, isoleucine, and valine along with their branched-chain alpha-ketoacids. Which enzyme complex is defective?
options: Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase
Propionyl-CoA carboxylase
Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
questions.correct_answer: Branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase
questions.explanation: Maple syrup urine disease results from deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex (a thiamine pyrophosphate-dependent enzyme analogous to pyruvate dehydrogenase), blocking oxidative decarboxylation of the branched-chain amino acid ketoacids and causing their accumulation, which gives urine its characteristic odor.

questions.question: A young adult with a Marfanoid body habitus, downward lens dislocation, and a history of thromboembolic stroke is found to have elevated plasma homocysteine and methionine but low cystathionine. Which enzyme deficiency explains this presentation, and what is the biochemical basis of the vascular risk?
options: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, because accumulated homocysteine promotes endothelial damage and thrombosis
Methionine synthase deficiency, because low methionine impairs collagen cross-linking
Homogentisate oxidase deficiency, because accumulated homogentisic acid deposits in connective tissue
Cystathionase deficiency, because elevated cystathionine is directly thrombogenic
questions.correct_answer: Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, because accumulated homocysteine promotes endothelial damage and thrombosis
questions.explanation: Cystathionine beta-synthase (a vitamin B6-dependent enzyme) normally condenses homocysteine with serine to form cystathionine; its deficiency causes homocystinuria, and elevated homocysteine is directly toxic to vascular endothelium, promoting thrombosis, along with lens dislocation and skeletal changes.

questions.question: A breastfed neonate develops jaundice, vomiting, hepatomegaly, and hypoglycemia after feeding begins, with a positive urine reducing substance test that is negative on the glucose-oxidase strip test. Which enzyme deficiency is most consistent with this pattern?
options: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase
Glucose-6-phosphatase
Fructokinase
Aldolase B
questions.correct_answer: Galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase
questions.explanation: Classic galactosemia is caused by GALT deficiency; lactose in breast milk is hydrolyzed to galactose and glucose, and accumulating galactose-1-phosphate is toxic to liver, kidney, and brain, while galactose itself gives a positive Clinitest (reducing substance) but negative glucose-specific dipstick result.

questions.question: After weaning onto fruit juice and table sugar, an infant develops severe hypoglycemia, vomiting, and abdominal pain specifically after consuming fructose-containing foods, with laboratory evidence of hypoglycemia disproportionate to the small carbohydrate load. Which enzyme deficiency, and what is the mechanism of the hypoglycemia?
options: Aldolase B deficiency; accumulated fructose-1-phosphate traps phosphate and secondarily inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
Fructokinase deficiency; fructose is entirely unmetabolized and osmotically diuresed
Glucokinase deficiency; glucose cannot be phosphorylated in the liver
Phosphofructokinase-1 deficiency; glycolysis is blocked at fructose-6-phosphate
questions.correct_answer: Aldolase B deficiency; accumulated fructose-1-phosphate traps phosphate and secondarily inhibits glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
questions.explanation: Hereditary fructose intolerance results from aldolase B deficiency; fructose-1-phosphate accumulates and sequesters inorganic phosphate, depleting ATP and inhibiting glycogen phosphorylase and gluconeogenic enzymes, producing severe hypoglycemia after fructose ingestion.

questions.question: A child with hepatomegaly and fasting hypoglycemia has a liver biopsy showing glycogen that is structurally normal but present in excessive amounts, with markedly elevated blood lactate, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia. Which glycogen storage disease enzyme deficiency fits, and why does severe lactic acidosis occur?
options: Glucose-6-phosphatase (von Gierke disease); glucose-6-phosphate cannot be released as free glucose and is shunted into glycolysis, generating excess lactate
Debranching enzyme; incomplete glycogenolysis directly produces lactate
Muscle phosphorylase (McArdle disease); exercise intolerance produces lactate
Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase (Pompe disease); glycogen trapped in lysosomes ferments to lactate
questions.correct_answer: Glucose-6-phosphatase (von Gierke disease); glucose-6-phosphate cannot be released as free glucose and is shunted into glycolysis, generating excess lactate
questions.explanation: Type I glycogen storage disease (von Gierke) results from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, blocking the final common step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; accumulated glucose-6-phosphate is diverted into glycolysis and the pentose phosphate pathway, causing severe lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, and hyperlipidemia alongside fasting hypoglycemia.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy develops muscle cramping and weakness only during brief bursts of intense exercise but has no rise in venous lactate during an ischemic forearm exercise test, and his urine turns dark (myoglobinuria) afterward. Which enzyme deficiency is implicated?
options: Myophosphorylase (muscle glycogen phosphorylase)
Liver glycogen phosphorylase
Pyruvate kinase
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
questions.correct_answer: Myophosphorylase (muscle glycogen phosphorylase)
questions.explanation: McArdle disease (type V glycogenosis) is caused by myophosphorylase deficiency; muscle cannot mobilize glycogen during anaerobic exercise, so venous lactate fails to rise on ischemic exercise testing, and rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria follows strenuous activity.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes is brought in confused and Kussmaul breathing, with blood glucose 480 mg/dL, arterial pH 7.15, serum bicarbonate 8 mEq/L, and strongly positive serum ketones. Which combination of hormonal changes best explains the ketoacidosis?
options: Insulin deficiency with elevated glucagon activates hormone-sensitive lipase and hepatic carnitine palmitoyltransferase I, driving fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis
Excess insulin suppresses lipolysis, forcing the liver to synthesize ketones from glucose
Elevated glucagon alone, without any change in insulin, directly converts glucose to acetoacetate
Cortisol deficiency prevents ketone clearance by peripheral tissues
questions.correct_answer: Insulin deficiency with elevated glucagon activates hormone-sensitive lipase and hepatic carnitine palmitoyltransferase I, driving fatty acid oxidation and ketogenesis
questions.explanation: In DKA, absolute insulin deficiency with unopposed glucagon activates adipose hormone-sensitive lipase, releasing free fatty acids, and lowers hepatic malonyl-CoA, relieving inhibition of carnitine palmitoyltransferase I so fatty acids enter mitochondria for beta-oxidation, generating excess acetyl-CoA that is converted to ketone bodies.

questions.question: In the same diabetic ketoacidosis patient, calculate the anion gap using Na+ 132 mEq/L, Cl- 92 mEq/L, and HCO3- 8 mEq/L, and classify the acid-base disturbance.
options: Anion gap 32 mEq/L, indicating a high anion gap metabolic acidosis
Anion gap 12 mEq/L, indicating a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
Anion gap 32 mEq/L, indicating a normal anion gap metabolic acidosis
Anion gap 8 mEq/L, indicating respiratory acidosis
questions.correct_answer: Anion gap 32 mEq/L, indicating a high anion gap metabolic acidosis
questions.explanation: Anion gap = Na+ - (Cl- + HCO3-) = 132 - (92 + 8) = 32 mEq/L, well above the normal 8-12 mEq/L range, consistent with accumulation of unmeasured ketoacid anions (beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate) in a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

questions.question: A patient with chronic diarrhea has arterial blood gas showing pH 7.30, HCO3- 15 mEq/L, and normal anion gap with hyperchloremia. What is the most likely explanation for the normal anion gap despite clear metabolic acidosis?
options: Bicarbonate lost in stool is replaced by retained chloride to maintain electroneutrality, so no unmeasured anion accumulates
Ketoacids are being buffered directly by chloride
Respiratory compensation has fully normalized the anion gap
Lactic acid accumulation is masked by concurrent alkalosis
questions.correct_answer: Bicarbonate lost in stool is replaced by retained chloride to maintain electroneutrality, so no unmeasured anion accumulates
questions.explanation: In diarrhea, bicarbonate-rich fluid is lost from the gut; the kidney retains chloride to preserve electroneutrality as plasma bicarbonate falls, producing a hyperchloremic, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis rather than one driven by an unmeasured organic acid.

questions.question: A marathon runner collapses near the finish line with muscle weakness. Blood gas shows pH 7.15, lactate 12 mmol/L (normal <2 mmol/L), and a high anion gap. Which metabolic shift explains the lactate elevation, and what enzyme becomes rate-limiting under these conditions?
options: Inadequate oxygen delivery forces pyruvate to be reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase to regenerate NAD+ for continued glycolysis
Excess oxygen delivery drives pyruvate dehydrogenase to overproduce lactate
Glycogen phosphorylase becomes inhibited, forcing anaerobic glycolysis
Citrate synthase deficiency shunts pyruvate to lactate
questions.correct_answer: Inadequate oxygen delivery forces pyruvate to be reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase to regenerate NAD+ for continued glycolysis
questions.explanation: When oxygen delivery cannot keep pace with muscular demand, the electron transport chain cannot reoxidize NADH fast enough; lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate, regenerating cytosolic NAD+ so glycolysis can continue to supply ATP anaerobically, at the cost of a rising lactate-driven high anion gap acidosis.

questions.question: A chronic alcoholic presents after a binge with hypoglycemia, elevated lactate, and metabolic acidosis, but minimal ketosis despite poor food intake. Which biochemical effect of ethanol metabolism best explains the hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis?
options: Ethanol oxidation via alcohol dehydrogenase raises the cytosolic NADH/NAD+ ratio, inhibiting gluconeogenesis and favoring conversion of pyruvate to lactate
Ethanol directly inhibits glycogen phosphorylase, preventing any glucose release
Ethanol stimulates insulin secretion, causing hypoglycemia independent of NADH changes
Ethanol is preferentially converted to glucose via gluconeogenesis, depleting oxaloacetate
questions.correct_answer: Ethanol oxidation via alcohol dehydrogenase raises the cytosolic NADH/NAD+ ratio, inhibiting gluconeogenesis and favoring conversion of pyruvate to lactate
questions.explanation: Alcohol dehydrogenase and aldehyde dehydrogenase generate large amounts of NADH, shifting the NADH/NAD+ ratio; this inhibits gluconeogenic reactions requiring NAD+ (such as conversion of lactate to pyruvate and malate to oxaloacetate) and pulls pyruvate toward lactate, producing hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis, while ketogenesis is often blunted by the altered redox state favoring beta-hydroxybutyrate over measurable acetoacetate.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man has recurrent tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus, and an LDL cholesterol of 310 mg/dL despite a normal diet; his father died of myocardial infarction at age 40. Which molecular defect most likely underlies this presentation?
options: Mutation in the LDL receptor gene impairing hepatic clearance of LDL particles
Deficiency of lipoprotein lipase impairing chylomicron clearance
Deficiency of apolipoprotein B-48 impairing chylomicron assembly
Overactivity of HMG-CoA reductase due to a gain-of-function mutation in the enzyme itself
questions.correct_answer: Mutation in the LDL receptor gene impairing hepatic clearance of LDL particles
questions.explanation: Familial hypercholesterolemia is classically caused by autosomal dominant mutations in the LDL receptor, which normally mediates hepatic uptake and clearance of LDL; reduced receptor function leads to markedly elevated plasma LDL-cholesterol, tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus, and premature coronary disease.

questions.question: An infant who was well between feeds becomes lethargic and hypoglycemic after a prolonged overnight fast, with inappropriately low serum ketones for the degree of hypoglycemia and mild hepatomegaly. Urine organic acids show medium-chain dicarboxylic acids. Which enzyme defect is most consistent with this picture?
options: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I deficiency causing excess ketogenesis
Pyruvate carboxylase deficiency
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
questions.correct_answer: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency
questions.explanation: MCAD deficiency blocks beta-oxidation of medium-chain fatty acids, so during fasting the body cannot generate adequate ketones as an alternative fuel (hypoketotic hypoglycemia), and partially oxidized fatty acids are shunted into omega-oxidation, producing medium-chain dicarboxylic aciduria.

questions.question: A researcher incubates isolated hepatocytes with radiolabeled palmitate and finds that adding malonyl-CoA sharply reduces the rate of ketone body production. Which enzyme is being inhibited by malonyl-CoA in this experiment, and what does this reveal about the regulation of fatty acid oxidation?
options: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I; malonyl-CoA allosterically inhibits it, coupling active fatty acid synthesis to suppression of fatty acid oxidation
Acetyl-CoA carboxylase; malonyl-CoA is itself the product, creating feedback inhibition of its own synthesis
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase II; malonyl-CoA binds the mitochondrial matrix side of the enzyme
HMG-CoA synthase; malonyl-CoA directly competes with acetoacetyl-CoA
questions.correct_answer: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase I; malonyl-CoA allosterically inhibits it, coupling active fatty acid synthesis to suppression of fatty acid oxidation
questions.explanation: Malonyl-CoA, the committed intermediate of fatty acid synthesis produced by acetyl-CoA carboxylase, allosterically inhibits CPT I on the outer mitochondrial membrane, preventing newly synthesized fatty acids from being immediately re-oxidized and ensuring that fatty acid synthesis and oxidation are not simultaneously active in the same cell.

questions.question: An enzyme assay is performed at increasing substrate concentrations with a fixed enzyme amount. A Lineweaver-Burk plot in the presence of a competitive inhibitor shows an unchanged y-intercept (1/Vmax) but an increased x-intercept magnitude (indicating a lower apparent Vmax... actually indicating increased Km). What does this pattern indicate about the inhibitor's mechanism?
options: The inhibitor binds reversibly to the free enzyme's active site, increasing the apparent Km while Vmax remains unchanged because sufficient substrate can still outcompete the inhibitor
The inhibitor binds only to the enzyme-substrate complex, lowering both Km and Vmax
The inhibitor binds irreversibly, permanently inactivating a fraction of enzyme molecules and lowering Vmax only
The inhibitor is an allosteric activator that increases substrate affinity
questions.correct_answer: The inhibitor binds reversibly to the free enzyme's active site, increasing the apparent Km while Vmax remains unchanged because sufficient substrate can still outcompete the inhibitor
questions.explanation: Competitive inhibition is characterized kinetically by an unchanged Vmax (the same 1/Vmax y-intercept) but an increased apparent Km, because high substrate concentrations can outcompete the inhibitor for the active site and still achieve maximal velocity, reflected as steeper slope lines converging on the y-axis in a Lineweaver-Burk plot.

questions.question: In a different kinetic experiment, an inhibitor decreases both the apparent Vmax and the apparent Km by the same proportion, so that Vmax/Km remains constant. Which type of inhibition does this represent?
options: Uncompetitive inhibition
Competitive inhibition
Pure noncompetitive inhibition
Irreversible inhibition
questions.correct_answer: Uncompetitive inhibition
questions.explanation: Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the enzyme-substrate complex, proportionally reducing both Vmax and Km (since removing ES complex pulls the equilibrium toward more ES formation, lowering apparent Km) while the ratio Vmax/Km, which reflects catalytic efficiency at low substrate, stays unchanged.

questions.question: A patient with chest pain has serum troponin I markedly elevated at 6 hours post-onset, while creatine kinase-MB peaks around 24 hours and lactate dehydrogenase remains elevated for several days. Which feature of these markers' release explains why troponin is now preferred over CK-MB for early diagnosis of myocardial infarction?
options: Troponin I is highly cardiac-specific and remains elevated for days, giving both early detection and a wide diagnostic window
Troponin I is present in skeletal muscle so it is less specific but more sensitive
CK-MB has a longer half-life than troponin, making it more useful for late diagnosis
LDH isoenzyme 1 rises before troponin and is now the preferred early marker
questions.correct_answer: Troponin I is highly cardiac-specific and remains elevated for days, giving both early detection and a wide diagnostic window
questions.explanation: Cardiac troponin I is a structural regulatory protein specific to cardiac myocytes; it rises within hours of myocardial injury and stays elevated for 7-10 days, offering both the specificity and the extended detection window that CK-MB (which peaks and normalizes faster and cross-reacts with skeletal muscle) cannot match.

questions.question: A patient with jaundice has elevated total bilirubin that is predominantly unconjugated, normal urine bilirubin (absent), elevated urobilinogen, and normal ALT/AST and alkaline phosphatase. Which category of jaundice is indicated, and what is the biochemical explanation for the absent urine bilirubin?
options: Prehepatic (hemolytic) jaundice; unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not water-soluble, so it is not filtered into urine
Hepatocellular jaundice; damaged hepatocytes fail to conjugate bilirubin at all
Posthepatic (obstructive) jaundice; conjugated bilirubin backs up but cannot reach the kidney
Gilbert syndrome cannot be distinguished from hemolysis using these values
questions.correct_answer: Prehepatic (hemolytic) jaundice; unconjugated bilirubin is albumin-bound and not water-soluble, so it is not filtered into urine
questions.explanation: Increased hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin production beyond hepatic conjugating capacity; unconjugated bilirubin is lipophilic and tightly albumin-bound, so it is not filtered by the glomerulus (acholuric jaundice), while increased bilirubin delivery to the gut raises urobilinogen, and liver enzymes remain normal since hepatocytes are not primarily affected.

questions.question: A patient with obstructive gallstone disease shows elevated conjugated (direct) bilirubin, dark urine, pale stools, elevated alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, with only mildly elevated ALT/AST. Explain the pale stool and dark urine findings biochemically.
options: Bile flow to the gut is obstructed, reducing stercobilin formation (pale stool), while conjugated bilirubin, being water-soluble, refluxes into blood and is filtered into urine (dark urine)
Increased hemolysis overwhelms the liver, producing both dark urine and pale stool
Conjugated bilirubin cannot be filtered by the kidney, so dark urine reflects hemoglobinuria instead
Alkaline phosphatase itself pigments the stool pale when elevated
questions.correct_answer: Bile flow to the gut is obstructed, reducing stercobilin formation (pale stool), while conjugated bilirubin, being water-soluble, refluxes into blood and is filtered into urine (dark urine)
questions.explanation: In obstructive jaundice, bile (and its conjugated bilirubin) cannot reach the intestine to be converted to urobilinogen/stercobilin, causing pale, clay-colored stools, while conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble and backs up into the bloodstream, where it is freely filtered by the kidney, producing dark urine.

questions.question: A severely malnourished 2-year-old presents with a distended abdomen, pitting edema, a fatty liver, and skin depigmentation, despite reasonable total caloric intake from a starchy, low-protein diet. Which biochemical mechanism best explains the edema and fatty liver in this presentation?
options: Inadequate protein intake lowers hepatic synthesis of albumin and apolipoproteins, reducing plasma oncotic pressure and impairing export of triglycerides from the liver as VLDL
Excess dietary carbohydrate is directly converted to edema fluid
Total caloric deficiency alone, independent of protein intake, causes both findings
Vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen synthesis, directly causing hepatic fat accumulation
questions.correct_answer: Inadequate protein intake lowers hepatic synthesis of albumin and apolipoproteins, reducing plasma oncotic pressure and impairing export of triglycerides from the liver as VLDL
questions.explanation: This is kwashiorkor: adequate calories but severe protein deficiency reduces hepatic protein synthesis, so albumin falls (causing edema via lowered oncotic pressure) and apolipoprotein B/VLDL assembly is impaired, trapping triglycerides in the liver as fatty liver, distinguishing it from marasmus (pure caloric deficiency with wasting but no edema).

questions.question: Comparing marasmus and kwashiorkor, a marasmic child typically has near-normal serum albumin and no edema despite severe wasting, while a kwashiorkor child has hypoalbuminemia and edema at a similar body weight deficit. What is the key biochemical distinction driving this difference?
options: Marasmus involves proportional deficiency of both calories and protein, allowing adaptive muscle protein catabolism to maintain visceral protein (albumin) synthesis, whereas kwashiorkor involves disproportionate protein deficiency that directly limits albumin synthesis
Kwashiorkor patients consume more calories overall, which paradoxically worsens albumin synthesis
Marasmus is caused by a vitamin deficiency unrelated to protein or calorie intake
Edema in kwashiorkor is caused by excess dietary sodium rather than any protein-related mechanism
questions.correct_answer: Marasmus involves proportional deficiency of both calories and protein, allowing adaptive muscle protein catabolism to maintain visceral protein (albumin) synthesis, whereas kwashiorkor involves disproportionate protein deficiency that directly limits albumin synthesis
questions.explanation: In marasmus, the body adapts to combined calorie-protein deficiency by breaking down muscle to supply amino acids for essential visceral protein synthesis, preserving albumin levels, whereas kwashiorkor's relatively isolated protein deficiency (with carbohydrate calories still available) does not trigger the same adaptive muscle catabolism, so albumin synthesis falls directly, producing edema.

questions.question: A chronic alcoholic with poor diet develops confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia (Wernicke encephalopathy). Which coenzyme deficiency underlies this presentation, and which enzyme's impaired activity best explains the neurological findings?
options: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency impairing alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase activity in neurons
Niacin deficiency impairing NAD+-dependent dehydrogenases throughout the body
Vitamin B12 deficiency impairing methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
Riboflavin deficiency impairing succinate dehydrogenase
questions.correct_answer: Thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency impairing alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and transketolase activity in neurons
questions.explanation: Thiamine pyrophosphate is an essential coenzyme for alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (TCA cycle), pyruvate dehydrogenase, and transketolase (pentose phosphate pathway); alcoholics are at risk of thiamine deficiency from poor intake and impaired absorption, and neurons, which are highly dependent on oxidative metabolism, are especially vulnerable, producing Wernicke encephalopathy.

questions.question: A patient on isoniazid therapy for tuberculosis develops peripheral neuropathy. Isoniazid is known to interfere with the activation of which vitamin, and how does this explain the neuropathy?
options: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6); isoniazid forms a hydrazone with pyridoxal phosphate, reducing its availability as a coenzyme for neurotransmitter and amino acid metabolism in nerves
Cobalamin (vitamin B12); isoniazid blocks intrinsic factor binding
Folate; isoniazid inhibits dihydrofolate reductase
Thiamine; isoniazid competes with thiamine for intestinal absorption
questions.correct_answer: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6); isoniazid forms a hydrazone with pyridoxal phosphate, reducing its availability as a coenzyme for neurotransmitter and amino acid metabolism in nerves
questions.explanation: Isoniazid structurally resembles pyridoxal phosphate's carbonyl-reactive site and forms an inactive hydrazone with it, functionally depleting active vitamin B6; since pyridoxal phosphate is required for synthesis of neurotransmitters like GABA, its depletion produces peripheral neuropathy, which is why isoniazid is co-administered with pyridoxine supplementation.

questions.question: A strict vegan with no B12 supplementation develops macrocytic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord with elevated serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine. A folate-deficient patient would show elevated homocysteine but normal methylmalonic acid. What explains this difference between the two deficiencies?
options: Vitamin B12 is a required coenzyme for both methionine synthase (homocysteine to methionine) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, whereas folate is required only for methionine synthase's methyl donation step
Folate deficiency does not affect homocysteine levels at all
Methylmalonic acid is elevated in folate deficiency but not B12 deficiency
B12 deficiency has no effect on methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
questions.correct_answer: Vitamin B12 is a required coenzyme for both methionine synthase (homocysteine to methionine) and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, whereas folate is required only for methionine synthase's methyl donation step
questions.explanation: Methylcobalamin is the coenzyme for methionine synthase (remethylating homocysteine using a methyl group from methyltetrahydrofolate) and adenosylcobalamin is the coenzyme for methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; folate deficiency impairs only the methionine synthase reaction (raising homocysteine) while leaving methylmalonyl-CoA mutase intact, so elevated methylmalonic acid specifically points to B12 rather than folate deficiency.

questions.question: A patient with untreated primary hyperthyroidism has weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, and tachycardia. Which cellular mechanism of thyroid hormone best explains the increased basal metabolic rate and heat production?
options: Thyroid hormone upregulates Na+/K+-ATPase expression and increases mitochondrial uncoupling, raising oxygen consumption and heat generation across tissues
Thyroid hormone directly inhibits the electron transport chain, generating heat as a byproduct of blocked respiration
Thyroid hormone acts solely by increasing insulin secretion, which raises metabolic rate
Thyroid hormone suppresses beta-adrenergic receptor expression, lowering heat production
questions.correct_answer: Thyroid hormone upregulates Na+/K+-ATPase expression and increases mitochondrial uncoupling, raising oxygen consumption and heat generation across tissues
questions.explanation: Thyroid hormone (T3) binds nuclear receptors and upregulates transcription of genes including Na+/K+-ATPase and uncoupling proteins, increasing ATP-consuming ion pumping and proton leak across the mitochondrial membrane, both of which raise oxygen consumption and thermogenesis, accounting for hyperthyroidism's hypermetabolic state.

questions.question: A patient with an insulinoma presents with episodes of confusion and sweating relieved by eating, and during a supervised fast, plasma glucose falls to 40 mg/dL while insulin and C-peptide remain inappropriately high. Why is C-peptide measurement useful here to distinguish an insulinoma from surreptitious exogenous insulin use?
options: Endogenous insulin is co-secreted with C-peptide from proinsulin cleavage in equimolar amounts, whereas exogenous insulin injections contain no C-peptide, so low C-peptide with high insulin indicates exogenous administration
C-peptide is only produced in response to exogenous insulin injection
C-peptide and insulin levels are unrelated and cannot distinguish these conditions
Insulinomas suppress C-peptide secretion while increasing insulin secretion
questions.correct_answer: Endogenous insulin is co-secreted with C-peptide from proinsulin cleavage in equimolar amounts, whereas exogenous insulin injections contain no C-peptide, so low C-peptide with high insulin indicates exogenous administration
questions.explanation: Proinsulin is cleaved into insulin and C-peptide in equimolar amounts within pancreatic beta cells; an insulinoma secretes both, giving high insulin with high C-peptide, whereas commercial insulin preparations lack C-peptide, so exogenous insulin use produces high insulin but suppressed (low) C-peptide due to feedback inhibition of endogenous secretion.

questions.question: A patient with Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) presents with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, and fasting hypoglycemia. Which two adrenal hormone deficiencies together best explain this full biochemical picture?
options: Aldosterone deficiency (causing sodium loss and potassium retention) combined with cortisol deficiency (impairing gluconeogenesis and glycogen mobilization)
Only cortisol deficiency, since aldosterone is unaffected in primary adrenal insufficiency
Only aldosterone deficiency, since cortisol does not affect glucose metabolism
Excess ACTH directly causing hyperkalemia independent of aldosterone or cortisol
questions.correct_answer: Aldosterone deficiency (causing sodium loss and potassium retention) combined with cortisol deficiency (impairing gluconeogenesis and glycogen mobilization)
questions.explanation: Primary adrenal insufficiency destroys the entire adrenal cortex, causing combined mineralocorticoid deficiency (loss of aldosterone-driven renal Na+ reabsorption and K+ excretion, producing hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and volume depletion) and glucocorticoid deficiency (cortisol normally supports gluconeogenesis and permits glucagon/catecholamine action, so its loss causes fasting hypoglycemia).

questions.question: Researchers feed rats 14C-labeled acetate and track radioactivity into cholesterol over several hours, then add a statin (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor) and repeat the experiment, observing a sharp drop in labeled cholesterol synthesis. This result best demonstrates which point in the cholesterol synthesis pathway?
options: HMG-CoA reductase catalyzes the rate-limiting, committed step converting HMG-CoA to mevalonate, so blocking it proportionally blocks downstream cholesterol synthesis from acetate-derived precursors
Acetate is not a precursor of cholesterol, so the drop reflects a nonspecific toxic effect
Statins block cholesterol absorption in the gut rather than acting on synthesis
HMG-CoA reductase acts downstream of squalene formation
questions.correct_answer: HMG-CoA reductase catalyzes the rate-limiting, committed step converting HMG-CoA to mevalonate, so blocking it proportionally blocks downstream cholesterol synthesis from acetate-derived precursors
questions.explanation: Acetate is converted via acetyl-CoA to HMG-CoA, and HMG-CoA reductase catalyzes the rate-limiting conversion of HMG-CoA to mevalonate, the first committed step of the cholesterol biosynthetic pathway; inhibiting this enzyme with a statin sharply reduces flux of labeled carbon from acetate into cholesterol, confirming its role as the pathway's control point.

questions.question: A pulse-chase experiment labels newly synthesized proteins with 35S-methionine in cultured hepatocytes, then follows a secretory protein over time using subcellular fractionation. Radioactivity appears first in the rough endoplasmic reticulum, then the Golgi apparatus, then secretory vesicles, and finally in the culture medium. What does this sequence demonstrate about the protein's biosynthetic pathway?
options: The protein follows the classical secretory pathway, being synthesized on membrane-bound ribosomes, processed and glycosylated through the Golgi, packaged into vesicles, and released by exocytosis
The protein is synthesized in the cytosol and diffuses freely into the extracellular medium
The Golgi apparatus is the final site of translation for secreted proteins
The rough endoplasmic reticulum is bypassed for secreted proteins in hepatocytes
questions.correct_answer: The protein follows the classical secretory pathway, being synthesized on membrane-bound ribosomes, processed and glycosylated through the Golgi, packaged into vesicles, and released by exocytosis
questions.explanation: The sequential appearance of label in RER, then Golgi, then vesicles, then medium traces the classical secretory pathway: signal-sequence-directed co-translational entry into the RER, post-translational modification and sorting in the Golgi, packaging into secretory vesicles, and release by regulated or constitutive exocytosis.

questions.question: A point mutation changes a codon for glutamate to a codon for valine in the beta-globin gene, producing hemoglobin S. Under low-oxygen conditions, deoxygenated HbS polymerizes into rigid fibers, distorting red cells into a sickle shape. What is the biochemical basis for this altered aggregation behavior?
options: The substitution replaces a charged, hydrophilic residue with a nonpolar hydrophobic one on the surface of the beta-globin chain, creating a hydrophobic patch that promotes intermolecular polymerization between deoxygenated hemoglobin molecules
The mutation destroys the heme-binding pocket, preventing oxygen binding entirely
The mutation introduces a premature stop codon, truncating the beta-globin chain
The mutation increases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, preventing normal unloading in tissues
questions.correct_answer: The substitution replaces a charged, hydrophilic residue with a nonpolar hydrophobic one on the surface of the beta-globin chain, creating a hydrophobic patch that promotes intermolecular polymerization between deoxygenated hemoglobin molecules
questions.explanation: The Glu6Val substitution on the surface of the deoxygenated beta chain creates a hydrophobic patch that fits into a complementary pocket on an adjacent hemoglobin tetramer, driving polymerization into long fibers specifically in the deoxygenated (low-oxygen) state, which distorts erythrocytes into the sickle shape.

questions.question: A patient with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency develops acute hemolytic anemia after taking an antimalarial drug. Which biochemical consequence of G6PD deficiency explains the red cells' vulnerability to oxidative drugs?
options: Reduced NADPH production limits regeneration of reduced glutathione, impairing the red cell's ability to detoxify peroxides and protect hemoglobin and membrane proteins from oxidative damage
G6PD deficiency directly destabilizes the red cell membrane cytoskeleton independent of oxidative stress
G6PD deficiency causes excess NADPH production, leading to oxidative damage
G6PD deficiency impairs hemoglobin synthesis, producing structurally unstable globin chains
questions.correct_answer: Reduced NADPH production limits regeneration of reduced glutathione, impairing the red cell's ability to detoxify peroxides and protect hemoglobin and membrane proteins from oxidative damage
questions.explanation: G6PD catalyzes the first, rate-limiting step of the pentose phosphate pathway, generating NADPH; red cells rely on this NADPH to keep glutathione in its reduced form via glutathione reductase, and reduced glutathione detoxifies peroxides via glutathione peroxidase, so G6PD deficiency leaves red cells unable to cope with oxidative stress from certain drugs, causing hemoglobin denaturation (Heinz bodies) and hemolysis.

questions.question: An experiment measures oxygen consumption of isolated mitochondria given succinate as substrate, then ADP is added and oxygen consumption rises sharply (state 3 respiration) before slowing once ADP is exhausted (state 4). When the uncoupler 2,4-dinitrophenol is then added, oxygen consumption rises again even without added ADP, and ATP synthesis stops. What does this demonstrate about the relationship between electron transport and ATP synthesis?
options: Electron transport and ATP synthesis are normally coupled via the proton gradient, and dinitrophenol dissipates this gradient, allowing electron transport (and oxygen consumption) to proceed independently of ATP synthesis
Dinitrophenol directly inhibits the electron transport chain, explaining the rise in oxygen consumption
ADP is not actually required for oxygen consumption in mitochondria
Uncouplers increase ATP synthesis by bypassing ATP synthase entirely
questions.correct_answer: Electron transport and ATP synthesis are normally coupled via the proton gradient, and dinitrophenol dissipates this gradient, allowing electron transport (and oxygen consumption) to proceed independently of ATP synthesis
questions.explanation: Chemiosmotic coupling links electron transport (which pumps protons and consumes oxygen) to ATP synthase activity via the proton-motive force; dinitrophenol is a protonophore that carries protons back across the inner membrane independent of ATP synthase, collapsing the gradient so electron transport can run freely (raising oxygen consumption) while no ATP is made, demonstrating that the two processes are mechanistically linked only through the proton gradient, not directly coupled biochemically.

questions.question: A patient with chronic kidney disease develops secondary hyperparathyroidism, with low serum calcium, elevated phosphate, and elevated parathyroid hormone. Which biochemical failure of the diseased kidney most directly triggers this cascade?
options: Reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity impairs conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to the active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, reducing intestinal calcium absorption and prompting compensatory PTH release
The kidney fails to filter parathyroid hormone, causing its direct accumulation
Reduced renal erythropoietin production directly lowers serum calcium
The kidney overproduces calcitonin, suppressing calcium reabsorption
questions.correct_answer: Reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity impairs conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to the active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, reducing intestinal calcium absorption and prompting compensatory PTH release
questions.explanation: The kidney performs the final activation step of vitamin D via 1-alpha-hydroxylase; in chronic kidney disease this activity falls, reducing active vitamin D and intestinal calcium absorption while phosphate retention also occurs due to reduced glomerular filtration, together driving hypocalcemia that stimulates compensatory parathyroid hormone secretion (secondary hyperparathyroidism).

questions.question: A neonate has severe hypotonia, hepatomegaly, and cardiomegaly, with a normal blood glucose but generalized muscle glycogen accumulation seen on biopsy, including glycogen trapped within lysosomes on electron microscopy. Which enzyme deficiency is implicated, and why is blood glucose normal despite glycogen accumulation?
options: Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase (Pompe disease); because cytosolic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis pathways remain intact, only the lysosomal glycogen degradation route is blocked
Glucose-6-phosphatase; because the enzyme defect spares muscle tissue entirely
Debranching enzyme; because debranching is not required for glucose release from glycogen
Muscle phosphorylase; because phosphorylase is not involved in glucose homeostasis
questions.correct_answer: Lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase (Pompe disease); because cytosolic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis pathways remain intact, only the lysosomal glycogen degradation route is blocked
questions.explanation: Pompe disease (type II glycogenosis) results from deficiency of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase, which normally degrades glycogen delivered to lysosomes by autophagy; because the cytosolic glycogen phosphorylase/debranching pathway that maintains blood glucose is unaffected, blood glucose stays normal, but glycogen progressively accumulates within lysosomes of cardiac and skeletal muscle, causing severe cardiomegaly and hypotonia.

questions.question: A woman in her third trimester of pregnancy develops nausea, right upper quadrant pain, and jaundice with markedly elevated ammonia, hypoglycemia, and microvesicular fatty liver on biopsy, without significant transaminase elevation typical of viral hepatitis. Her fetus is later found to have a deficiency in an enzyme of fatty acid oxidation. Which maternal-fetal biochemical mechanism best explains the mother's acute fatty liver of pregnancy?
options: Fetal long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency causes accumulation of toxic long-chain fatty acid metabolites that cross into maternal circulation and overwhelm maternal hepatic fatty acid oxidation capacity
Maternal insulin resistance alone, unrelated to fetal enzyme status, fully explains the liver findings
The fetal enzyme deficiency has no biochemical connection to maternal liver disease
Excess fetal ketone production is transferred to the mother, directly causing her hepatic failure
questions.correct_answer: Fetal long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency causes accumulation of toxic long-chain fatty acid metabolites that cross into maternal circulation and overwhelm maternal hepatic fatty acid oxidation capacity
questions.explanation: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is associated with fetal LCHAD deficiency; abnormal long-chain fatty acid intermediates produced by the affected fetus/placenta enter the maternal circulation and are thought to overwhelm the mother's mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation capacity (especially heterozygous carrier mothers), producing microvesicular hepatic steatosis, hypoglycemia, and hyperammonemia resembling other fatty acid oxidation defects.

questions.question: A biochemist measures the activity of an allosteric enzyme (analogous to phosphofructokinase-1) and plots reaction velocity against substrate concentration, obtaining a sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic curve. What does this sigmoidal shape indicate about the enzyme's subunit behavior?
options: Cooperative binding among multiple subunits, where binding of substrate to one site increases the affinity of other sites for substrate
The enzyme obeys simple Michaelis-Menten kinetics with a single substrate-binding site
The enzyme is irreversibly inhibited at low substrate concentrations
The sigmoidal curve indicates the enzyme has no allosteric regulation
questions.correct_answer: Cooperative binding among multiple subunits, where binding of substrate to one site increases the affinity of other sites for substrate
questions.explanation: A sigmoidal velocity-versus-substrate curve is the signature of positive cooperativity in multi-subunit allosteric enzymes: initial substrate binding induces a conformational change that increases the affinity of remaining subunits, producing a steep rise in activity over a narrow substrate concentration range, in contrast to the hyperbolic curve of simple Michaelis-Menten enzymes.

questions.question: A patient taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor eats aged cheese and experiences a hypertensive crisis. Which biochemical interaction explains this reaction?
options: MAO inhibition prevents breakdown of dietary tyramine in the gut and liver, allowing it to reach sympathetic nerve terminals and trigger massive norepinephrine release
MAO inhibitors directly convert tyramine into a vasodilator
Aged cheese contains excess sodium that raises blood pressure independent of MAO
MAO inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme, indirectly raising blood pressure
questions.correct_answer: MAO inhibition prevents breakdown of dietary tyramine in the gut and liver, allowing it to reach sympathetic nerve terminals and trigger massive norepinephrine release
questions.explanation: Monoamine oxidase in the gut and liver normally degrades dietary tyramine (abundant in aged cheese) before it enters systemic circulation; when MAO is inhibited, tyramine reaches sympathetic nerve terminals intact, displacing stored norepinephrine and triggering its massive release, precipitating a hypertensive crisis, the classic 'cheese reaction.'

questions.question: A researcher studying an inherited metabolic disease finds that fibroblasts from an affected patient show normal enzyme activity when assayed in a test tube (in vitro) with excess exogenous cofactor, but the patient still shows clinical symptoms of the deficiency in vivo. What does this pattern most likely suggest about the underlying molecular defect?
options: The mutation affects cofactor binding affinity or cellular cofactor transport/availability rather than the enzyme's catalytic mechanism itself, so supplying excess cofactor in vitro masks the defect
The patient does not actually have the enzyme deficiency, and the diagnosis should be reconsidered
The enzyme assay technique is inherently invalid for inherited metabolic diseases
The defect must be in an unrelated gene with no connection to the enzyme being studied
questions.correct_answer: The mutation affects cofactor binding affinity or cellular cofactor transport/availability rather than the enzyme's catalytic mechanism itself, so supplying excess cofactor in vitro masks the defect
questions.explanation: Some inherited enzyme deficiencies are 'cofactor-responsive,' where the mutation lowers the enzyme's affinity for its cofactor (a vitamin-derived coenzyme) rather than destroying catalytic activity outright; providing pharmacologic excess cofactor in vitro (or clinically, as in some vitamin-responsive inborn errors) can restore near-normal activity by mass action, even though physiological cofactor concentrations in vivo are insufficient.

questions.question: A patient in septic shock has arterial blood gas: pH 7.32, PaCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3- 14 mEq/L. Using Winter's formula, expected PaCO2 = 1.5(HCO3-) + 8 (+/-2). Does the measured PaCO2 represent appropriate respiratory compensation, and what does the result imply?
options: Expected PaCO2 is 29 (+/-2) mmHg, and the measured value of 28 mmHg falls within this range, indicating appropriate respiratory compensation for a primary metabolic acidosis
Expected PaCO2 is 40 mmHg, so the measured value indicates a superimposed respiratory alkalosis
Winter's formula does not apply because the pH is not low enough to confirm acidosis
The measured PaCO2 indicates a primary respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
questions.correct_answer: Expected PaCO2 is 29 (+/-2) mmHg, and the measured value of 28 mmHg falls within this range, indicating appropriate respiratory compensation for a primary metabolic acidosis
questions.explanation: Winter's formula predicts expected PaCO2 = 1.5(14) + 8 = 29 mmHg (range 27-31); the measured PaCO2 of 28 mmHg falls within this predicted range, confirming that the respiratory system is appropriately hyperventilating to compensate for the primary metabolic acidosis (likely lactic acidosis from sepsis), with no independent respiratory disorder.

questions.question: A patient with persistent vomiting from pyloric stenosis develops a blood gas showing pH 7.52, HCO3- 34 mEq/L, and elevated PaCO2 of 48 mmHg with hypokalemia and paradoxical aciduria. Explain why the urine is acidic despite systemic alkalosis.
options: Volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, promoting renal H+ and K+ secretion to conserve Na+, so the kidney excretes acidic urine even though the body is alkalotic
The kidney is directly generating new bicarbonate that is excreted as acid
Loss of gastric acid should make urine alkaline, and acidic urine indicates a laboratory error
Hypokalemia has no effect on renal acid-base handling
questions.correct_answer: Volume depletion activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, promoting renal H+ and K+ secretion to conserve Na+, so the kidney excretes acidic urine even though the body is alkalotic
questions.explanation: Loss of HCl in vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis, but the accompanying volume depletion activates aldosterone, which enhances distal nephron Na+ reabsorption in exchange for K+ and H+ secretion; combined with hypokalemia driving intracellular-to-extracellular H+ shifts and enhanced renal H+ excretion, the kidney paradoxically excretes acidic urine while systemic pH remains alkalotic, a hallmark of contraction alkalosis.
